articleTitle: Project cost and schedule risk analysis
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Risk Analysis Methods and Tools
abstract: Uncertainty is an inevitable feature of planning, and traditional techniques of network and resource analysis can do little to overcome it. Two simple initiatives can help a lot though. There are: formal steps to identify and quantify risks; and simple quantitative risk modelling. Together they make up a risk analysis process working along side conventional planning methods. Inexpensive software tools are now available for risk modelling. The author briefly discusses their benefits and then discusses the use of probabilistic models in cost and schedule risk modelling.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Risk Analysis Methods and Tools
abstract: The discipline of safety engineering uses a wide variety of terms to describe the many techniques that are available to it which can be generally collected within the heading of risk and hazard management. The author defines what is meant by risk analysis and discusses the main factors governing the need to conduct risk analysis. Three examples of the application of risk analysis are discussed: a hazardous industry; a rail system; and risk analysis as a design assessment support for a wind turbine generator. The author briefly discusses how to interpret the risk analysis data.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Embedding risk-management in process models II
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Risk Analysis Methods and Tools
abstract: The author presents a straightforward view of the development of a process model. Two candidates for activities within the process model are envisaged: the end-system and the process itself. The author discusses process model influences, the origins of risk, the TRIAD building system, and the development of risk managed process models.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The risk reduction plan. A positive approach to risk management
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Risk Analysis Methods and Tools
abstract: The author sets out the need for risk management, and describes how the risk reduction plan (RRP) provides the solution. Two case studies are included to illustrate how the plan may be put into operation. The first case study illustrates the use of a RRP to help prepare a bid, and the second case illustrates the use of a RRP to obtain approval for the plans included in the bid.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Risk Analysis Methods and Tools
abstract: The author describes a technique referred to as security modelling which, although it does not set out with the same aims as risk analysis, has wide applications in the study of risk, is much simpler to use, and is more general. The technique is based around a software tool and draws upon ideas from reliability engineering, risk analysis and spreadsheets. Its main features are: it places the user in the active role; it enables models of the security features of an organisation to be built and freely experimented upon; it automatically uncovers all possible destructive combinations of events implied by the model, including those not foreseen by the user; it unifies into a single concept the notions of asset, threat, vulnerability and countermeasure; and it enables joint optimisation of cost and effectiveness.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Engineers and risk issues: the Engineering Council Code of Practice
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Risk Analysis Methods and Tools
abstract: The Engineering Council has prepared a Code of Good Practice for its registrants, setting out what is expected of their conduct in respect of engineering risk issues. It gives advice and support to registrants, but is also a reference against which professional conduct can be judged, both by the council and by the public at large. It will form the centrepiece of a major initiative by the Council to raise awareness in industry, government and education of the vital role of systematic risk assessment and management if disasters are to be avoided. The author discusses the background issues to the code and its content including the 10 point code of practice.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: IEE draft guide to the practice of system engineering (third draft)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Risk Analysis Methods and Tools
abstract: The 'Guide to the Practice of System Engineering' is an aid to the system engineer in his/her professional practice. The system engineer can turn to the Guide for a check-list of activities for reassurance and guidance on the approach to system engineering and its relationship with other engineering activities. The Guide identifies the role of system engineering; the aim and objectives of system engineering; the activities needed to satisfy the aim and objectives; and the basis for coherent training of system engineers. The Guide is related to project engineering and management and represents an approach to risk management.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Risk analysis techniques in defence procurement
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Risk Analysis Methods and Tools
abstract: The author explains the risk analysis techniques used by the Accountancy, Estimating and Pricing Services (AEPS), Ministry of Defence, Procurement Executive. The aim of the author is to provide a convenient reference document for procurement staff rather than to advance the theory. Topics covered include identification of risk areas, approaches to risk analysis and strategies for risk reduction and control. The choice of risk analysis technique depends on the definition, scale and phase of the project. All techniques, however, require a systematic approach, so a generalised methodology for risk analysis is proposed. Whilst risk analysis methods and models are valuable tools, the right answers still depend upon judgment and specialist expertise.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
